title: It Rained Gold on Bombay
description: The Fort Stikine explosion, Victoria Dock, Bombay, 14 April 1944.

lines.text: It rained gold on Bombay.
Real gold bars, falling out of the sky.
One smashed into this man's home.
What he did next, almost nobody would do.
But first: where did the gold come from?
It's April 14, 1944. World War Two.
A British cargo ship, the Fort Stikine,
is tied up in Bombay's Victoria Dock.
In her holds: about fourteen hundred tons of explosives.
Torpedoes, mines, shells.
Eight thousand seven hundred bales of raw cotton.
And thirty-one crates of gold.
The cotton is packed underneath the explosives.
And she isn't flying the red flag that warns of danger on board.
At twelve-thirty,
an officer on the next ship
sees smoke coming out of hold number two.
The hold with the gold.
It's more than an hour before anyone raises the alarm.
Firemen race in.
Fireboats pull alongside.
They pour more than nine hundred tons of water into the ship,
and still can't find the fire.
Down in the hold, the shells start going off.
At three-fifty comes the order: abandon ship.
Sixteen minutes later.
Four-oh-six p.m.
The Fort Stikine explodes.
The ship is torn in two.
The blast throws another ship, the Jalapadma,
out of the water and onto the dock.
Windows shatter twelve kilometres away.
In Shimla, seventeen hundred kilometres away,
instruments feel the ground shake.
Burning cotton falls across the city.
And with it, gold.
Less than half an hour later, a second explosion.
Thirteen ships are lost.
The docks burn for three days.
More than seven hundred people are killed.
Eighty thousand lose their homes.
Sixty-six of the dead are firemen.
That's why, every April 14th,
India marks National Fire Service Day.
And the gold bar in Girgaum?
Its owner carries it to the police.
They reward him nine hundred and ninety-nine rupees.
He gives every rupee to the relief fund for the victims.
And the gold kept turning up.
As late as 2011,
dredgers in Bombay's docks were still pulling
the ship's gold bars out of the mud.
